slides.title: Resampling and Interpolation About changing the frequency of
slides.text: Resampling and Interpolation About changing the frequency of your observation Upsampling: increase frequency of observations Ex: Going from monthly observations to daily observation Question of how to fill in the missing values Usually use a line or a polynomial to connect two points Downsampling: decrease frequency of observation Same idea as above, but now we are going from monthly measurements, to quarterly observations Usually use means to get the summarized data

slides.title: Power Transforms Data transforms are intended to make
slides.text: Power Transforms Data transforms are intended to make time series stationary and remove trend Square Root Transform: A time series that has a quadratic growth trend can be made linear by taking the square root. Log Transform: Time series with an exponential distribution can be made linear by taking the logarithm of the values. Box-Cox Transform: The Box-Cox transform is a configurable data transform method that supports both square root and log transform, as well as a suite of related transforms. it can be configured to evaluate a suite of transforms automatically and select the best fit. See boxcox () function Ex: Square Root Power Transform Notice the quadratic trend. By taking the square root of every term in the original time series, we can remove the quadratic trend

slides.title: Moving Average Smoothing Technique applied to time series
slides.text: Moving Average Smoothing Technique applied to time series to remove the fine-grained variation between time steps (removes noise) Calculating a moving average involves creating a new series where the values are comprised of the average of raw observations in the original time series Two different techniques: Centered moving average: center ma(t) = mean( obs (t - 1); obs (t); obs (t + 1)) Trailing moving average: trail ma(t) = mean( obs (t - 2); obs (t - 1); obs (t)) Use Python’s rolling( window_size ) function to achieve this

slides.title: Time Series Components Systematic: Level, Trend, Seasonality Non-Systematic:
slides.text: Time Series Components Systematic: Level, Trend, Seasonality Non-Systematic: Residual y(t) = Level + Trend + Seasonality + Residual        (additive) y(t) = Level Trend Seasonality Residual     (multiplicative) Statsmodels library provides automated decomposition tools

slides.title: Noise Signal(t) = level + trend + seasonality
slides.text: Noise Signal(t) = level + trend + seasonality + noise A time series is white noise if the observations are independent and identically distributed with a mean of zero. => complete random error Filtering on horizontal and vertical scale Check basic stats for noise type Ex: White noise (complete random)

slides.title: Using and Removing Trend/Seasonality Trends: deterministic vs. stochastic,
slides.text: Using and Removing Trend/Seasonality Trends: deterministic vs. stochastic, global vs. local Time series with trend = non-stationary Use augmented Dickey-Fuller test to check for stationarity Why do we care? Removing or Adding Information to ML Model Detrend by Differencing : value(t) = observation(t) - observation(t-1) Detrend by Model Fitting : value(t) = observation(t) - prediction(t)

slides.title: AR I MA (a.k.a. Box-Jenkins Model) Autoregressive Integrated
slides.text: AR I MA (a.k.a. Box-Jenkins Model) Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average Model Three Steps: Identify model that best summarizes the data Use data to train the model Diagnostic checking. How good is the fitted model? Notation: ARIMA(p, q, d) p = lag order , number of lag observations included in model q = difference order, number of times the raw observations are differenced To remove trend and make time series stationary d = order of moving average , size of moving average window

slides.title: Autoregressive (AR) Models Models an output value as
slides.text: Autoregressive (AR) Models Models an output value as a linear combination of input variables (similar to linear regression): Assumes autocorrelation ( is directly related to ) and stationarity Example of Lag plot Example of autocorrelation plot

slides.title: AR Model Details: Assumption: Forecast series without trend/seasonality
slides.text: AR Model Details: Assumption: Forecast series without trend/seasonality AR(p): AR model of order p Similar to linear regression. But predictors are lagged versions of the series Plus parameters are estimated differently (not using least squares) The currently observed value of Y is some linear function of its past p values Forecast :

slides.title: Integrated Apply differencing to detrend time series data
slides.text: Integrated Apply differencing to detrend time series data Models build on stationary data are usually more robust Thus, we aim for mean variance stationarity Future change in Y is a linear function of the past changes in Y

slides.title: Moving Average Model Residuals provide another piece of
slides.text: Moving Average Model Residuals provide another piece of information we can use to model the data Forecasts Y using the model’s past errors This model is called moving average model!! Don’t’ confuse with moving average smoothing Modelling the time series of the errors to improve forecast!

slides.title: How does it work? Create Integrated Autoregressive model
slides.text: How does it work? Create Integrated Autoregressive model Get residuals: residuals = test_y – predictions I - This gives us a time series of residual errors. II - Then model these residual errors using normal autoregression to obtain coefficients & 	      intercept 3. Walk through each time series data point and: I – calculate AR prediction (t+1) II – Predict residual error using autoregressive model III – Update residual errors time series lag values so we can calculate next error 4. Correct initial predictions from AR model with forecasted errors from the autoregressive model I – Improved forecast = Old AR Forecast + New Estimated Error Forecast II – Ex: if Autoregressive model predicted value of 8, but our AR Model of the errors 	predicted an error of 3 for this time stamp, we would have an updated prediction of 8 + 3 = 	11 Training of the model is done iteratively. Training process goes through multiple steps.

slides.title: Tips: Use differencing to remove trend and seasonality
slides.text: Tips: Use differencing to remove trend and seasonality Keep it Simple! Over differencing can cause problems. “In most cases either p is zero or q is zero, and p + q is less than or equal to 3 ” Duke Prof. Robert Nau (http:// people.duke.edu /~ rnau /411home.htm)

slides.title: AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA, ARIMAX, SARIMAX Great explanation:
slides.text: AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA, ARIMAX, SARIMAX Great explanation: .. https://towardsdatascience.com/understanding-arima-time-series-modeling-d99cd11be3f8 More links: .. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoregressive%E2%80%93moving-average_model .. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoregressive_integrated_moving_average .. https://www.statsmodels.org/dev/examples/notebooks/generated/statespace_sarimax_stata.html .. https://365datascience.com/tutorials/python-tutorials/sarimax/ .. https://people.duke.edu/~rnau/411arim.htm Autoregressive Model: - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5-2C4eO4cPQ - Autocorrelation and Partial Autocorrelation - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DeORzP0go5I - ACF and PACF: - https://towardsdatascience.com/significance-of-acf-and-pacf-plots-in-time-series-analysis-2fa11a5d10a8 .. https://people.duke.edu/~rnau/411arim.htm ARIMA(p, d, q) = ARIMA (AR, I, MA) p = number of lagged values in AR model (number of autoregressive terms) d = order of differencing (used for stationarity) q = number of lagged errors in MA model ARIMA(1,0,0)  - 1st order autoregressive model ARIMA(2,0,0)  - oscillations ARIMA(0,1,0)  - random walk ARIMA(1,1,0)  - differenced first-order autoregressive model ARIMA(0,1,1)  - simple exponential smoothing: ARIMA(0,1,1)  - simple exponential smoothing with growth ARIMA(1,1,1) - ... ARIMA(0,2,1)  - linear exponential smoothing ARIMA(0,2,2)  - linear exponential smoothing AR = Auto-Regressive (next point as linear combination of several previous) Y_forward1 = B0 + B1*Y + B2*Y_lag1 + ... MA = Moving Average Y = B0 + B1*E_lag1 + B2*E_lag2 + ... + Bn*E_lagn , where "E" =  residual errors (which change as we iteratively train the model) "I" = Integrated (use differences to remove trend while modeling): Y_forward1 - Y = B0 + B1*(Y - Y_lag1) + B2*(Y_lag1 - Y_lag2) + ... ARMA = AR + MA = Auto Regressive Moving Average model ARIMA = AR + I + MA = Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average model "X" = eXogenous variables (additional variables, think " multivariate regression ") ARIMAX = ARIMA with exogenous variables. An exogenous variable is a covariate that influence the observed time-series values SARIMAX = Seasonal ARIMAX – includes seasonal factors ACF = Auto-Correlation Function PACF = Partial ACF SARIMAX
